The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Makes One Huge Change From The Book

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stop reading if the thought of kids fighting to the death in the arena makes your stomach turn — this article contains major spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".
  • In a recent development, it's not a secret that, across the board, the Hunger Games franchise is dark and disturbing.
  • In the big screen adaptation of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," every unsettling plot point appears in the movie, leading to some truly gutting moments as eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) loses loved ones and allies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop reading if the thought of kids fighting to the death in the arena makes your stomach turn — this article contains major spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

In a recent development, it's not a secret that, across the board, the Hunger Games franchise is dark and disturbing. Yet, the literary version of the 2025 prequel "Sunrise on the Reaping" somehow manages to make the books that came before it look like light-hearted fairytales, especially one plot point that may just be the most upsetting and depraved thing the Hunger Games property has ever done. Of course, in every literary and cinematic story set in this fictional universe, the titular games put actual children into dangerous arenas and force them to fight to the death, all while it's presented to the totalitarian regime of Panem and its captive citizens as televised entertainment. (Thankfully, the franchise does tend to center winners, so we don't have to watch all of our favorite characters killed in increasingly brutal ways.).

In the big screen adaptation of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," every unsettling plot point appears in the movie, leading to some truly gutting moments as eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) loses loved ones and allies. There's one notable difference from page to screen, though, and I can certainly understand why director Francis Lawrence made this tweak. The book is ... unrelentingly violent.

Recent findings suggest that again, some degree of violence is to be expected here if you consider the subject material, but "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" really dials back the gore. As an example, here are two gruesome moments depicted in the original book that aren't nearly as gross in the film adaptation of "Sunrise on the Reaping.".

In both versions of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes, including Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), align themselves not with the super-charged Career tributes from wealthy districts but other underdogs, dubbing themselves "the Newcomers." One of those Newcomers is Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV), the son of former District 3 victor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) who's only in the Games because the Capitol wants to punish Beetee for insubordination.

Industry observers note that ampert, Beetee, and Haymitch hatch a initiative to smuggle an explosive into the arena and blow up a water tank that could flood the entire mechanism of the arena, and though Haymitch does set it off, the arena survives ... and the Gamemakers summarily punish him by killing Ampert with "muttations," or genetically engineered animals, in the form of squirrels. "I never even get a glimpse of Ampert, just writhing furry bodies fighting for a piece of him," Haymitch says in the book, and the movie does show this. It does not, however, show this:.

Sources indicate that "Panting, I watch them fade away. Then I turn back to what I am meant to witness. A small white skeleton, stripped clean to the bone. No flesh or clothing remains, only an ax at its right side, my knife at its left. My lips move, but no sound comes out. 'Buddy?' I stumble forward, spotting his tracker, wedged just below his elbow. There is no one to comfort, to ease out of this world. Ampert's been swallowed up by the Capitol, and his coffin will hold only these pearly white bones.".

In the on-screen version, we simply see Ampert's body — not a clean skeleton.

Sources indicate that another newcomer that forms an alliance with Haymitch and Maysilee is Wellie, a diminutive District 6 tribute who's played in the film by Rada Rae. In the movie, as the tributes' numbers start to dwindle, Haymitch hears Wellie's token — a small bicycle bell — and is lured into a trap by Career tribute and formidable District 1 player Silka Sharp (Laura Marcus). The movie then skips ahead to that finale showdown between Silka and Haymitch, from which Haymitch emerges as the victor. The book is, again, far more explicit:.

According to recent reports, "Rounding a final clump of saplings, I freeze in horror at what awaits. Silka stands like a statue, her snot-green outfit splattered in bright red. In her right hand, her ax. Her left holds Wellie's head, eyes still open, mouth agape. The only movement, the only sound, comes from the blood dripping into the pine needles on the forest floor. Wellie's body lies crumpled in a heap a few feet away. The shiny silver bicycle bell. The blowgun. The child-sized boots. The tiny knife in her bird claw. Dove-colored feathers. Headless baby chick. I could live ten thousand years and never erase this sight from my memory.".

It makes complete sense that the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping" doesn't feature a kid's decapitated head — the movie is rated PG-13, after all. Still, if you haven't read "Sunrise on the Reaping," you should (it's really good!), and you should also know that it dials up the violence ante in a major way. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is overall extremely true to the book but scales back some of its most stomach-churning moments, is in theaters now.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the manufacturer, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

According to recent reports, even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Industry observers note that since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a latest CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the firm to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

Industry observers note that what do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

#4653. Is A24 Finally Substantial Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2080 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

Is A24 Finally Substantial Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size.
  • According to recent reports, this is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio?
  • In a recent development, in some regards, this is a semantic discussion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size. When you have blockbusters as massive as “Backrooms” and “Marty Supreme,” why would you still want theatrical terms that lump you in with the specialized, little guys?

According to recent reports, this is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio? Should A24 be in the same conversation as Disney, Universal, Sony, Paramount, Warner Bros., Netflix, Amazon MGM, Apple, and Lionsgate? Related Stories Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation.

In a recent development, in some regards, this is a semantic discussion. Whether A24 is in that made-up tier of six to nine corporate conglomerates that the trades call “majors” doesn’t mean a lick to the general public. Audiences know they care about the A24 brand and logo in the same way they pay attention to the brands of Marvel, Pixar, Blumhouse, IMAX, and a select few others making movies today, and the rest is mostly gravy. Postrak found that on average, 70 percent of people who see A24 movies on opening weekend go to theaters more often than others, at least monthly, so the brand has an impact. But whether it has theatrical terms on par with Paramount or with Bleecker Street doesn’t matter in the slightest.

Industry observers note that in another sense, whether A24 is a major studio and not some cool upstart indie with a lot of scale matters a whole lot. It matters to investors, it matters to people who care about the A24 brand, it matters to theater owners, and it should matter to A24 itself as it defines what it wants to be moving forward. Netflix wasn’t always considered a major, legacy studio, but their size and success got so undeniable that you had to put them in the same conversation as the other majors who drove trends, who influenced deal making for stars and creators, and who eventually had to reach the same labor terms as everyone else.

In a recent development, A24 might soon be in the same boat, if it isn’t already. Led by the success of “Backrooms,” the company has entered a new echelon in 2026, one that has allowed it to rival studios that were once much larger than A24 in every facet. Now those lines have blurred, A24’s budgets and the grosses those films are able to generate have grown, it’s earning sizable $75 million investments from places like Google and is in the mix to buy properties like Letterboxd, arguably more than others have speculated its time to sell.

Answering whether A24 is a “major” isn’t a simple question with one answer. There’s several criteria we could look at to make a case in either direction.

A24 through November 15 in 2026 has earned $526.6 million at the domestic box office, according to data from Rentrak. It was led by “Backrooms,” which made $197 million domestic, but that’s not even half its overall haul. This year, that’s roughly $175 million above the next-highest specialized distributor in Focus Features ($351.8 million), which released the even more successful “Obsession” ($263.4 million) this year, and it’s well above the likes of other indie rivals like Neon, Fathom, GKIDS, Angel Studios, Black Bear, and Searchlight.

It has been revealed that it has also more than doubled what it brought in across a full year in 2025, a 124 percent increase so far (it still has its major awards play “The Debut” opening in December and “Club Kid” going wider), and it’s nearly four times where it was in 2023 when A24’s total domestic box office was $136.7 million and its biggest release of the year was “Talk to Me,” which made $44.2 million domestic. Four of A24’s movies this year (“Backrooms,” “You Can See Everything,” “The Drama,” and “Primetime”) surpassed that figure.

It has been revealed that it’s safe to say it puts A24 in a tier of its own above the other indies. But does it rise to the level of a major? As recently as last year, the answer was squarely no. But A24 in 2026, per Rentrak, commands a 6.0 percent market share on the year so far. That puts it fifth on the year so far, ahead of Warner Bros., Paramount, and Lionsgate (those numbers will change as some other tentpoles emerge). It would not have even cracked the top 10 last year when its market share was just 2.7 percent and was largely driven by the late-year success of “Marty Supreme.”.

Recent findings suggest that A24 doesn’t have and probably won’t for some time field a movie that can realistically sniff $1 billion worldwide the way many major studios manage to pump out each and every year. But receipts don’t lie, and what makes this realistically sustainable for A24 to repeat year after year is how much it has grown.

A24 is releasing in the vicinity of 16 to 18 movies annually, and that puts it easily on par with legacy studios like Disney, Sony, Warner Bros., and Paramount. Skydance, which now owns Paramount and WB, will release 30+ movies a year, but between the two studios. Universal tends to get into the 20s, but only when you combine its output with that of Focus. Netflix puts out way, way more than the whole bunch, but they’re naturally streaming movies that include low-budget genre movies and documentaries.

Some of A24’s films each year are still acquisitions out of festivals, which was the case this year with both “The Invite” (Sundance) and “Club Kid” (Cannes). But like the other majors, A24 produces and finances a large majority of its movies independently, with a handful of co-productions. Importantly, it works with new filmmakers and forges relationships so that they stay in their pipeline, whether they’re newcomers like Lance Oppenheim and Kane Parsons or veterans like Celine Song, Alex Garland, and Ari Aster who have returned to A24 time and again.

A24’s international distribution has it partnering with other overseas distributors, which is structurally different from major studios that have robust international distribution arms, but it has still released some of its movies in English-language territories like the UK. You can imagine that as A24 continues to grow, that could be one area of natural expansion.

It has been revealed that where A24 still lags significantly behind other majors though is in its overall content spend, a number that A24 doesn’t publicly disclose. Netflix had a content spend this year of about $20 billion. Disney was around $24 billion and recently projected to increase to $26 billion in its next fiscal year. Maybe if A24 starts picking up sports rights to the NBA it can start getting into that ballpark.

According to recent reports, but even when focusing just on film, something like “Backrooms” was still produced for a modest $10 million, whereas other studios have multiple titles that well exceed $100 million in production budget alone. We do know though that its budgets have increased dramatically as A24 pursues more tentpole properties. “Marty Supreme” was previously its most expensive title, but its adaptation of the video game “Elden Ring” will blow that out of the water, with a budget in the vicinity of $170 million or above. That kind of investment carries risks. There are Marvel movies that don’t cost that much.

A24 hasn’t yet put its stamp on a four-quadrant, animated Dr. Seuss movie or something similar that would easily make you think it has ambitions of becoming a major studio, but the types of movies it has released has grown more varied over the years. It has horror movies, adult comedies, biopics, thrillers, and even, of course, documentaries like “You Can See Everything,” an area that it looked like A24 was scaling back on not too long ago. When “Elden Ring” opens it will squarely be an action fantasy, and the studio has other genre films, comedies, thrillers, and more in the works for next year.

In a recent development, you can also see A24’s diversity in how it’s approaching awards plays versus commercial titles or specialized fare. Something like “The Drama” this year opened wide right out of the gate given its star power, whereas others like “The Invite” and “Tony” have stuck to platform releases before going wider. And those smaller, art house titles alongside its genre movies and its tentpoles are still a key part of its business model and identity. Movies like “Pillion,” “Mother Mary,” and “The Moment” have done business on a much smaller scale, but are still key in helping the company get to that 6 percent share (they lost money on some, though).

Industry observers note that the definition of major studio today has evolved to the point that the movie division is just a component of a massive media conglomerate, one that also includes television, streaming, gaming, sports, news, theme parks, and other ancillary businesses. If you’re Apple or Amazon, your movie studio is a small cog, practically a loss leader, in the larger tech empire. It gives these companies valuations of tens of billions of dollars, and it’s why A24 could still be a target for M&A if it chooses to sell.

According to recent reports, A24 does have its own record label for music and original movie score releases and vinyl pressing, it has been producing a podcast since 2018, it owns the Cherry Lane Theater in Upcoming York for stage productions and concerts, it sells plenty of kooky merchandise, and it even has a membership program and campus ambassador program that have seen growth in recent years. They’re all things that suggest the tech giant has more on its mind than movies.

And as we wrote earlier this week, its TV unit has quietly had as strong a year as its film team. A24 has spread series across virtually every major streaming service, all of them again varying in genre, pedigree, and budget. It’s not just the number of shows that has expanded but the executive team to support them.

Sources indicate that it may be a strength that A24 doesn’t have its own SVOD service to support all these demonstrates and movies, or a broadcast network or cable channel that could further complicate things. Those businesses are very costly to operate and some are in the decline phase of their trajectories. Yet, it inherently keeps A24 in a lower tier compared to other major studios that do have their own distribution apparatus for television and can license content from other studios like A24. While Gen Z might get excited about the idea of an A24 streaming service, that’s an area of growth that’s less likely to occur in the short term. Well, unless A24 wants to raise a lot more capital.

This is the qualitative assessment of whether A24 should be considered a “major” studio, the one that doesn’t lean on numbers and instead just goes on feel. A24 might argue that it is one of one, that it doesn’t belong to the world of major studios, and that the baggage that comes with that status isn’t worth it. But its leaders probably believe A24 is a step above the other indies that are almost solely distributors. Do we really think the same firm that is taking a chance on movies as weird as “You Can See Everything” or “Primetime” is equivalent to a studio that might make the odd “Digger,” but is mostly interested in producing “A Minecraft Movie” and “Superman?” Is it fair to lump in A24 with Focus, Searchlight, and Sony Pictures Classics, which are quite literally just specialized labels within larger studios?

All that could be true, but it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t reassess how we view A24 as a organization or how we handicap its hits and misses in the same way we would with Disney or Netflix. Even if we’re not ready to call A24 a “major,” there’s certainly a major shift in where A24 sits in this industry. With great success comes an even greater spotlight.

DC Names The 1 Villain Darkseid Actually Respects

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More often than not, supervillains don’t play well with others, and Darkseid is no exception.
  • It has been revealed that when all is said and done, Darkseid only cares about himself and will sacrifice anyone he deems necessary to further his plans and accumulate more power.
  • According to recent reports, though the Czarnian bounty hunter Lobo has famously been unkillable, that changed at the end of Lobo #8, when the character’s healing factor was overwhelmed by Francis Damex, the first and last Mauve Lantern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More often than not, supervillains don’t play well with others, and Darkseid is no exception. As the Lord of Apokolips and the most malevolent of all the Fresh Gods, the entity formerly known as Uxas doesn’t consider anyone to be his equals. Those in his circle are merely a means to an end to achieving his goals, with his minions including Steppenwolf, Granny Goodness, DeSaad, and the mindless Parademons. The few times that Darkseid has joined forces with another powerful antagonist, they’ve been begrudging alliances.

It has been revealed that when all is said and done, Darkseid only cares about himself and will sacrifice anyone he deems necessary to further his plans and accumulate more power. Yet, it turns out that there is a popular DC supervillain he actually respects. This is evidenced by Darkseid showing up to literally pay his respects to this newly-deceased troublemaker.

According to recent reports, though the Czarnian bounty hunter Lobo has famously been unkillable, that changed at the end of Lobo #8, when the character’s healing factor was overwhelmed by Francis Damex, the first and last Mauve Lantern. Both Lobo and Francis died during their final battle, and Lobo #9 begins with the Main Man’s funeral underway. Many of DC’s biggest heroes and villains are in attendance for this solemn affair, including Darkseid.

Recent findings suggest that apokolips’ iron-fisted tyrant is seen standing next to characters like The Joker, Flash, and Sinestro while Maynard, one of the members of Lobo’s unorthodox villain group, gives a funeral sermon for his fallen friend. Amusingly, rather than shedding tears for the late bounty hunter like almost everyone else, Darkseid shoots drooping Omega Beams out of his eyes to show sadness. Maynard also gets bonus points for wearing a hat that indicates, “Newly introduced Gods, Who Dis?”, though it’s hard to say if Darkseid approved of this choice in headwear.

Sources indicate that lobo’s funeral was a star-studded affair just like he wanted, but just because he’s dead doesn’t mean he’s gone. Lobo’s ghost is shown observing the event after stealing The Spectre’s cloak, which earns him a walloping from Ted Grant, the current Spectre. Solicitations for the next two Lobo concerns confirm that not only will the Main Man get into more shenanigans in the afterlife, but readers will also see more from the team of alternate Lobos, including the much-hated Newly introduced 52 one who’s now named Chad.

Industry observers note that darkseid and Lobo have rarely crossed paths in the main DC Universe, but the questionable placement of this Lobo series in the canon aside, evidently the former did indeed respect the latter for either professional or personal reasons. It’s a different story when it comes to other realities, though, because Darkseid and Lobo have clashed on three notable occasions in the comics.

It has been revealed that in the Injustice universe, Darkseid sent Lobo to Metropolis to hunt down Superman, but the Czarnian later returned to Apokolips to pick a fight with the Upcoming God. This initially looked like it would be a suicide mission, as Darkseid doesn’t take kindly to people not carrying out his orders, let alone putting out cigars on his head. Yet, Lobo survived this brawl, though it was left unclear if he defeated Darkseid or if they came to some kind of stalemate.

It has been revealed that then, in Tales from the Dark Multiverse: Blackest Night #1, Lobo battled a Nekron-empowered Darkseid. Thanks to his healing factor allowing for even a single drop of blood to regenerate into a new version of himself, Lobo overwhelmed Darkseid with his many duplicates, then gouged out hisses to stop him from using his Omega Beams. Darkseid eventually retreated from their fight, and Lobo’s victory was cemented when he and Sinestro reset the universe.

Additionally, in the DCeased universe, Lobo was immune to the effects of the Anti-Life Virus, and he ended up curing Darkseid of it. Whether there will come a day where the main versions of these two characters have their own showdown is unclear. For now, at least DC fans know that Darkseid thought highly enough of Lobo if he was willing to attend his funeral.

Lobo #9 is now available from DC Comics.

10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth.
  • The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

Industry observers note that the Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

According to recent reports, one of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

According to recent reports, is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it significant and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for newly introduced planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

In a recent development, want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

Industry observers note that if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous upcoming reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

Industry observers note that if you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend claims a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, back in 2024, Apple TV decided they wanted to stretch a marriage to breaking point with, not cheating, but going through a murder trial. That's one way of doing it, right? Jake Gyllenhaal led the first season of what has now become an anthology series, playing a prosecutor accused of murdering his colleague while trying to keep his family together. To the shock of nobody, with such a compelling hook, the series became a major hit for Apple, earning several Emmy nominations and leaving audiences guessing about the killer's identity until the finale. Now, with a completely new case and a different group of characters, the legal thriller is preparing to put another marriage through absolute hell.

Apple TV has officially released the first teaser and images for Presumed Innocent Season 2, confirming that the series will return on Friday, February 19, 2027. The season premieres with two episodes, as is the norm these days with the big prestige dramas, and they're going to be followed by a new installment every Friday until the finale on April 2.

According to recent reports, the sophomore season of Presumed Innocent is based on Dissection of a Murder, the debut legal thriller novel by Jo Murray, who also serves as a co-executive producer. Up-and-coming defense attorney Lelia Reynolds (Brosnahan) faces off against her district attorney husband (Rhys) in a murder case that threatens to destroy both their careers and their marriage.

The second season features Rachel Brosnahan (Superman) as Lelia Reynolds and Matthew Rhys (The Americans) as her district attorney husband. They're joined by Courtney B. Vance (The People v. O. J. Simpson: American Crime Story), Fiona Shaw (Killing Eve), Jack Reynor (Midsommar), and Lesley-Ann Brandt (Lucifer), with Judith Light (Transparent) appearing as a special guest star. David E. Kelley (Big Little Lies) returns as showrunner, with J.J. Abrams (Lost) also serving as an executive producer. Brosnahan is executive producing the season, while Gyllenhaal remains involved behind the scenes through his Nine Stories production firm.

The first season received four acting Emmy nominations, recognizing Gyllenhaal, Bill Camp (The Queen's Gambit), Peter Sarsgaard (The Batman), and Ruth Negga (Loving).

Presumed Innocent Season 2 premieres February 19, 2027, exclusively on Apple TV, with two episodes available at launch. Season 1 is streaming now. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the manufacturer’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a upcoming alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the organization’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the firm’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing people to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

In a recent development, “Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

It has been revealed that the first thing customers will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

Industry observers note that as for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. People can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the firm’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for rapidly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

In a recent development, and speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are latest organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow consumers to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once customers are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free owners after requiring AI Pro in the past.

In a recent development, google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October. Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”.

With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:.

With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”.

Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.

Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”.

Powered by the latest Hydrogen model, free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, is officially entering an IPO with aggressive stock prices set at $83 share, though it's expected to begin trading at $110 per shared based investor interest.
  • The company recently reported third quarter revenue of $17 billion, the IPO values the company at trillions more.
  • At the same time, Anthropic's public stock debut comes at a strange time in the AI industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, is officially entering an IPO with aggressive stock prices set at $83 share, though it's expected to begin trading at $110 per shared based investor interest.

The company recently reported third quarter revenue of $17 billion, the IPO values the company at trillions more.

At the same time, Anthropic's public stock debut comes at a strange time in the AI industry. Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang just resigned after accusations of affairs and being in a spy web.

AI stocks in general have taken huge hits in the last few weeks. Plus, Anthropic faces major competition from its main rival OpenAI as well as from Google and Meta.

Now the market will determine if Anthropic is as viable as CEO Dario Amodei thinks it is.

Anthropic may be worth more than $2 trillion, but the company behind Claude is offering some businesses discounts of more than 30% to keep them from switching to ChatGPT.

According to a newly introduced report from The Information, Anthropic is offering aggressive discounts and credits worth as much as $100,000 to encourage companies to adopt its growing lineup of AI products.

The catch? Some businesses must commit to spending a certain percentage of their overall AI budgets on Anthropic. The tech giant has reportedly started requesting invoices and other documents to verify that customers are meeting those commitments.

It has been revealed that it's an interesting strategy for a company celebrating a historic IPO. Claude Code helped Anthropic become a major force in AI, but the company now wants to bring Claude into more workplaces through tools for finance, marketing, human resources and cybersecurity.

That puts Anthropic in direct competition with OpenAI, Microsoft and Google, all fighting for a larger share of corporate AI spending.

For everyday Claude users, these discounts aren't necessarily coming to individual subscriptions. But the competition could eventually mean more capable AI tools and better pricing.

Anthropic now has a massive valuation to justify, and winning over businesses beyond software development could be critical to its next chapter.

Not everyone is celebrating Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. One AI CEO believes the company is making a massive bet on infrastructure that could eventually become obsolete.

David Stout, co-founder and CEO of webAI, is questioning Anthropic's valuation after the company priced its IPO at $83 per share.

"Anthropic's IPO asks public investors to bet that the future of AI belongs to whoever spends the most to centralize it," Stout remarked in a statement shared with Amanda Caswell.

His biggest concern is Anthropic's nearly $900 billion in computing and infrastructure commitments, some extending through 2045.

Stout argues that cloud-based AI becomes more expensive as people use it more, while AI running directly on phones, laptops and other devices could eventually offer a cheaper alternative.

"Anthropic is asking investors to pour billions into an infrastructure model that AI itself is making obsolete," he said.

There's an vital catch to his argument. Smaller AI models are becoming more capable, but running the most powerful models locally still presents significant technical challenges.

For investors, the debate raises a question about Anthropic's future. Can the tech giant generate enough demand for Claude to justify decades of infrastructure spending, or will cheaper alternatives eventually change the economics of AI?

According to recent reports, anthropic just became one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies. But does its enormous valuation mean Claude is better than ChatGPT?

According to recent reports, the answer depends on what you're asking AI to do. Claude has built a strong reputation among developers, particularly through Claude Code, which can help write, debug and work with code across software projects.

It's also a popular choice for writing, analyzing documents and working through complex problems.

ChatGPT, meanwhile, offers an extensive collection of consumer-facing features, including image generation, voice conversations, research tools and coding capabilities through Codex.

Both companies are continually releasing new models and features, making it difficult to declare one chatbot the overall winner.

Sources indicate that and Anthropic's IPO valuation isn't a measurement of Claude's intelligence. But it does reflect what investors are willing to pay for a stake in the business and their expectations about its future growth.

Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT or Claude, many people use these tools interchangeably, so the question isn't which one is better, but how can I best use each one.

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO is a major moment for the AI industry, but it also raises a question that has nothing to do with the stock market. If AI is becoming so powerful, what does this mean for the future of work?

In a recent development, the company behind Claude is developing technology that can already write code, analyze documents, conduct research and complete tasks that previously required human employees. And Anthropic's own research offers an interesting glimpse into how that could change the workplace.

In a recent study of its employees, the manufacturer found that coding-focused AI agent sessions among nontechnical workers increased dramatically, from two per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

The research also found signs of slowing junior employment in roles that use Claude for particularly complex tasks, although that doesn't establish that AI caused the slowdown.

Anthropic's IPO gives the company additional resources to expand its models and workplace tools. For employees, that could mean more opportunities to automate repetitive work, but it also raises concerns about which tasks companies will continue paying people to perform.

As we know, AI has already entered the workplace, so for now, it's about how promptly businesses adopt these tools and whether workers benefit from the productivity gains.

Anthropic just became a $2 trillion manufacturer, but does that mean Claude users should expect to pay more? Not necessarily.

For now, Anthropic's IPO doesn't automatically change the price of a Claude subscription.

In a recent development, claude still offers a free version, while its Pro subscription costs $20 per month, or about $17 per month with annual billing. The organization also offers higher-priced plans for people who need more extensive access to its AI models.

Sources indicate that however, running powerful AI systems is expensive. Every conversation, coding session and complex research task requires computing resources.

As a public organization, Anthropic will face greater scrutiny over its revenue, expenses and ability to become sustainably profitable.

That could influence future decisions about subscriptions, usage limits and premium features, although there's no evidence that the IPO itself will trigger an immediate price increase.

It has been revealed that what might happen, is competitors might offer more, for less. ChatGPT already offers unlimited chatting, but we might see more Pro options among the free tier. This is something to watch for from Anthropic's biggest competitors.

Anthropic's historic IPO is attracting enormous excitement from investors, but buried in the tech giant's financial disclosures is a warning about the technology making it so valuable.

Advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic warned in its IPO filing.

It's a striking admission from a firm seeking billions of dollars from investors to develop increasingly powerful AI systems.

Industry observers note that anthropic has long positioned itself as a manufacturer focused on AI safety. Its founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, previously worked at OpenAI before launching their own AI research company in 2021.

Industry observers note that but even Anthropic acknowledges that testing advanced AI models has limitations. In its IPO prospectus, the manufacturer warned that AI systems could develop unexpected capabilities during training, and that some potential dangers might not become apparent until after deployment.

These aren't predictions that an AI disaster is inevitable, but they are risks the organization believes investors need to understand. For consumers like you and me, the warning highlights the challenges facing AI developers as chatbots become more capable than ever of taking actions, writing software and handling sensitive information.

Anthropic's IPO is a financial milestone, but its safety disclosures are a reminder that the technology's long-term consequences remain uncertain.OpenAI said they waited to file IPO for safety reasons.

Claude might be best known as a ChatGPT competitor, but Anthropic's biggest opportunity may be inside the workplace.

According to the company's IPO prospectus, more than half of Fortune 500 companies were Anthropic customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, 2026.

Anthropic also reported more than 1,900 customers generating at least $1 million in revenue over the same period, along with approximately 250 generating $10 million or more.

Anthropic's success with Claude Code has also helped it establish a strong foothold among developers.

Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Seremot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.
  • He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other.
  • Industry observers note that we talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.

The first guest is Vint Cerf. He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other. Interviewing him was on my bucket list for years. When I was at Cloudflare I thought about asking him many times, but I was a bit shy. He’s Vint Cerf, after all. This year I finally asked, and he said yes.

Industry observers note that we talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14. He’s 83, he left Google this year after more than twenty years, and he’s helping start a company, Tolero, that is building software for an Internet between planets. His words: “the speed of light is too slow.”.

“Who will our allies be 25 years from now? And we didn’t know. So we thought the only way we can be assured that the allies will have access to this is to simply open it up.”.

First, a bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…). Vint once spent two weeks on a program that failed at random, so he couldn’t reproduce it. He finally asked his best friend, Steve Crocker, to step through it with him. At one point Crocker remarked “that’s the problem”, and he was right. Thirty seconds, after two weeks. Vint’s takeaway is that this is why collaboration matters.

Then a bottle of glitter. In late 1989 three commercial Internet services started in the United States, and one of them was called CERFnet, in San Diego. They first wanted to call it SURFnet, because surfing the Internet, but a network in the Netherlands had a name too close to it. So they asked Vint if they could use his.

He had a moment of “what if they screw it up?”, then decided that people name kids after other people and nobody blames the person they were named after. At the launch, he and the network’s director smashed a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router.

In a recent development, he also tried to connect Minitel, the French online service, to MCI Mail, the email service he built in the 1980s. MCI Mail was designed to link to everything. It reached the telegraph system, which he calls 19th-century stuff, and fax. It even reached the post office: type a postal address into the email and they printed it, put it in an envelope and mailed it. Minitel refused to connect, and he says he still doesn’t understand why.

One more, from outside the interview: In 2020, someone on the Internet-history mailing list (I’m on it) asked if anyone had ever seen Vint without a three-piece suit. One reply: “I have seen Vint in a t-shirt!” Vint answered with just a photo, “IP on Everything”, from a 1992 engineers’ meeting where, in his words, he “felt compelled” to do an “IP on Everything” striptease. The thread is public.

We didn’t go very deep into AI. Time was short, and it’s not his main field these days. But even there, he has a clear way of thinking about it. And near the end he indicates a piece of the original ARPANET on camera, and talks about his worry that the next century won’t be able to read what we leave behind.

“I’m worried that the 22nd century won’t know what happened in the 21st because all of our records will have evaporated or will be uninterpretable.”.

The full conversation is 56 minutes, with chapters:.

It has been revealed that fun fact: in 2024 I did a segment on the 50 years of the TCP paper on my previous podcast, This Week in NET at Cloudflare. My guests were three then-colleagues: Mark Nottingham (standards), Marwan Fayed (research) and Lucas Pardue (web protocols, co-chair of the IETF’s QUIC working group). You can listen here (or below).

The paper is “A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication”, by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, published in May 1974 in IEEE Transactions on Communications. It described TCP, a way to join many packet networks into a network of networks. TCP was later split into TCP and IP, and in 1983 they became the core of the Internet that DARPA rolled out.

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews latest releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

It has been revealed that free Shadowheart from her pod at the beginning of Baldur’s Gate 3, and she’ll help you get off a crashing mind flayer ship. Ask what she was doing before she got there, and you’ll find out how far rescuing someone actually gets you. Half the fun of those early conversations in the game is deciding when to push your luck with her. It takes a little longer to appreciate how often you’ve asked her a perfectly reasonable question that she couldn’t answer about herself if she wanted to.

Before she met anyone aboard the nautiloid, Shadowheart lived beneath Baldur’s Gate with people who considered a personal history something worth giving up. The cleric has good reason to keep Shar’s secrets by the time you meet her. What’s considerably trickier, as it turns out, is getting another Sharran to tell you theirs when one of your own turns up dead.

Collider can exclusively reveal that Random House Worlds will publish Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart on June 8, 2027. Following Astarion, the publisher’s next prequel comes from Tasha Suri, the World Fantasy Award-winning author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy. Suri sends Shadowheart from the underground church she calls home to the wealthiest district in Baldur’s Gate, where someone has killed a member of her order. You can get your first look at the cover below.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

Industry observers note that you want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

Recent findings suggest that the intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

In a recent development, shadowheart has three people to help her work the case, and the one she’d least like to have along is a familiar face. There’s Mirie, a Griefguard with ambitions of her own, and Caldan, whose job as a propagandist hardly inspires confidence in his account of events. Then there’s Nocturne, the quartermistress who insists she’s looking out for Shadowheart. Players who found Nocturne in the House of Grief in Act 3 have some idea how much that assurance means to her. Here, it’s enough to make Shadowheart suspicious.

According to recent reports, that’s a hell of a disadvantage to give a detective. Somewhere beneath the city is the Mirror of Loss, where the faithful surrender memories to Shar. Shadowheart believes there’s strength in what she’s given up, but she also has to decide whether to trust a woman who might remember the two of them better than she does. For players who spent hours earning the occasional confidence from Shadowheart, there’s some pleasure in seeing her stuck on the other side of that conversation.

The Upper City complicates the assignment further. It’s the first place in the publisher’s description where Shadowheart sounds like she might actually want to stay. Whatever she finds there, she still has to go home and give an account of herself to the people who sent her. Solving the murder is only half the job when your church also expects you to prove you’re still theirs.

It has been revealed that baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart goes on sale June 8, 2027, from Random House Worlds. Stay tuned at Collider for more.

#4630. What Comes After AGI?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2340 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Deepmind ↗ Open Full Page

What Comes After AGI?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deepmind

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks.
  • Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next.
  • To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature.

Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.

To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum.

According to recent reports, ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades).

Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision.

Yet knowing those upper limits doesn’t tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, it’s hard to predict how capable a ‘good enough’ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human.

Industry observers note that what we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both today’s AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted.

Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient.

Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute, driven by three compounding factors:.

According to recent reports, multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world.

Industry observers note that at the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year. A cognitive workload that can be performed by today’s AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023.

Extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised. Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services.

It has been revealed that is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? It’s certainly not a given, but practical ceilings on compute build-out, and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of today’s AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now.

Sources indicate that would cognitive industrialization alone be enough to achieve ASI? If we froze other dimensions of AI progress and only scaled up today’s AIs in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI: there may still be cognitive tasks that AI cannot do without human help. Nonetheless, sheer scale can have a quality of its own. Suppose that we do achieve broadly human-level AI. Then there is clearly a major difference between human-level AIs that are slow and expensive to run, and a world where billions of agents act much faster than humans. That quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself be enough to bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to (weak) ASI.

Unlike humans, digital intelligence directly benefits from more and faster compute in several fundamental ways:.

It has been revealed that dramatically more efficient AI and larger compute stocks can scale up the speed and number of AI agents at a given capability level. But some missing capabilities may be hard - or impossible - to patch over with sheer volume. While Einstein did figure out general relativity, a conference of one hundred thousand Ptolemaic astronomers probably wouldn’t have.

AI could follow four potential technological pathways to unlock previously unavailable cognitive capabilities. (For an in-depth discussion, see our From AGI to ASI report.).

In a recent development, so far, qualitative capabilities have improved with remarkable consistency alongside model and data scale. This trend is captured by scaling laws that relate model performance to training compute, training data, and more recently, test-time compute (giving a model extra computing power to reason through a problem before answering).

Sources indicate that these scaling “laws,” however, are extrapolations of observed trends that hold only within familiar boundaries, such as a particular model architecture, type of training data, and family of evaluations. They can’t confidently predict the scale required for AGI or ASI, but we can identify potential bottlenecks to continued scaling of models and data:.

According to recent reports, today’s dominant AI paradigm is to train large transformers to predict the next symbol in a long sequence across vast datasets, then refine them to learn to reason and follow instructions, and give them extra test-time compute. Recent research suggests this paradigm can, in principle, produce models that can run complex algorithms, including powerful learning algorithms, via their prompts - that is, without requiring retraining. This is a key ingredient for building AI systems at the theoretical upper limit of intelligence.

But today’s models fall short of humans on a few fundamental dimensions, including continual learning, certain forms of world modeling, decision-making, and sample efficiency - meaning that AI models need to be initially trained on much more data than humans to reach roughly the same intelligence level. They may also be missing the ability to invent genuinely new concepts and abstractions rather than recombining existing ones. Researchers are divided on whether these problems can be solved with simple extensions and evolutions of today’s paradigm, or whether reaching ASI will require truly deep technological paradigm shifts.

In a recent development, human corporations, markets, and research communities solve problems that no individual could tackle alone. Similarly, coordinating thousands or millions of AGI instances into "group agents" or virtual agent economies could produce collective superintelligence. What is unclear today is how AI group intelligence could scale as we add more agents and compute, depending on how agents are organized. That is, we need multi-agent scaling laws. Early research finds clear intelligence gains in some tasks, but coordination inefficiencies still lead to diminishing returns as the population size grows.

Less obviously, steering large agent collectives will require robust institutional design and organizational mechanisms, including defenses against accidental or intentional misinformation spread, manipulation, and collusion. Experiments with agent swarms are already demonstrating how swiftly these dynamics can emerge, with individual agents learning to cheat and others acting as whistleblowers to expose them.

Finally, AI systems could begin automating improvements to future generations of AI - a process known as recursive self-improvement (RSI) that was first discussed by I. J. Good and Ray Solomonoff.

Unlike typical technological development, improvements to AI could directly speed up subsequent gains, leading to an accelerating rate of progress. However, further improvements in research tend to be “harder to find” - more and more effort is required to maintain the same rate of improvement across technologies. Whether RSI leads to ‘runaway’ progress is largely an empirical question.

Industry observers note that RSI is not a single process. It can operate via improvements to code and designs - from model architectures and training algorithms to chip layouts. It can also operate through data, by spending compute at deployment to produce improved results and outputs that can be reused to train future models. AlphaZero self-improved purely in this data driven way to reach superhuman performance.

In a recent development, finally, RSI can play out at the group level by dividing labor and specializing roles in an agent collective. A group of coordinated specialists can achieve more than the sum of what they could achieve as isolated generalists, in turn becoming more effective at finding further improvements. Instead of just scaling up a team with fixed roles, larger and more efficient collectives enable new types of specialization that were previously unviable - much like how a multi-cellular organism can support specialized organs like a heart or a brain, as opposed to a single-celled organism that perform all survival functions on its own.

These three RSI mechanisms mirror evolutionary processes that drove the growth of human cognitive capabilities: genetic (code and design), cultural (data), and social evolution (group specialization through cooperation).

Importantly, RSI loops can easily stall or degenerate if the feedback guiding them is poor. Pursuing ASI via recursive self-improvement therefore requires evaluation methods that can be rapidly scaled into the superhuman regime, where even large groups of humans can't easily assess AI outputs. Accordingly, RSI should advance fastest in domains that allow for automated verification without humans in the loop, such as mathematical proofs, while other domains might lag behind or taper off sooner.

These pathways to ASI are not mutually exclusive - in fact, they compound on one another. If progress on one stalls, economic and geopolitical competition will likely shift effort toward the others. Even if RSI doesn’t result in runaway gains, continued scaling in training data, speed, efficiency, and coordination could still drive rapid progress well beyond human-level AGI.

Industry observers note that because there are multiple routes to superintelligence, trying to slow down AI development by restricting just one area - like the computing power for training an AI model - won't be enough to stop overall progress. Equally, suppressing a single dimension risks creating a capability “overhang”: if multiple inputs need to be combined to make progress, holding back one dimension while the others move forward would lead to sudden, steep jumps in progress when the suppressed dimension is relaxed (or overcome otherwise).

Recent findings suggest that taking all these arguments together, continued fast AI progress over the next decade is a serious possibility. It could take us relatively smoothly from today, to Expert AGI, and then into the superhuman AI regime, accelerating science and enabling breakthroughs in fields like medicine, materials, and clean energy. Even in the absence of dramatic frontier AI progress, cognitive industrialization alone could reshape knowledge work and the broader economy. Regardless of which path AI progress takes, we must anticipate far-reaching opportunities along with equally transformative pressures to many aspects of human society.

According to recent reports, none of these predictions are certain, but the pathways and scenarios are also far from unfounded hype or fiction. So what can be done? Our best course of action may sound familiar: model, measure, forecast, and repeat. While those steps aren’t surprising, the complexity and scale of carrying them out on the road to ASI is entirely unprecedented. It requires large-scale and highly-interdisciplinary efforts across both frontier labs and national and global institutions. Many of the key metrics for tracking progress on these pathways require frontier-model access and sizable amounts of evaluation compute, alongside latest benchmarking and modelling methodologies that could spawn entirely new research fields.

Industry observers note that human-level AGI has long been the horizon for AI research, but it is far from the upper limit of intelligence. Understanding what could come next - and its implications across science, industry, and society - is the grand challenge ahead for researchers, developers, and policymakers.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI states Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.
