📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover upcoming powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

In a recent development, if you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:.

In an existing git repository, run:.

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:.

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:.

According to recent reports, in addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:.

According to recent reports, A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

Recent findings suggest that when using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

Industry observers note that the IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:.

On commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:.

Industry observers note that jj show shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here. $ jj show Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) Committer: Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) (no description set).

According to recent reports, jj status shows repo state with diff stats. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config.

Sources indicate that jj diff works much like git diff. Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

Sources indicate that this output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show, we see this:.

It has been revealed that you’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty). The fresh commit ID for @ is 66b59f20, since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon. jj has no staging area like in git, so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc, which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m.

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

It has been revealed that now, let’s say we’re ready to use this new feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new:.

We’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon. jj status reflects that we are editing this new revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj latest combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

To inspect the commit we just created (n), we can no longer use the bare jj show, which defaults to showing @. We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:.

It has been revealed that we can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a new commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj upcoming. Here’s the current commit graph:.

Note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj’s branchless model and git’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

Recent findings suggest that A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj latest k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Commits between r and @, inclusive:.

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:.

Recent findings suggest that I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

It has been revealed that let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon. We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit:.

Our working copy once again demonstrates the changes from kpqxywon.

jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q:.

Instead of switching commits with jj edit k, we could have run jj edit @-. The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

Industry observers note that if we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get newly introduced commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit….

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted:.

Let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git, undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj, we can always run jj undo:.

More generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log. We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo.

The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Sources indicate that let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a new commit on top of the conflicted commit:.

Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log:.

We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:.

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

Sources indicate that one of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo, we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

In a recent development, let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.

According to recent reports, let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit (q) should go between the implementation (k) and the usage (n). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz:.

In a recent development, another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well.

Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below k, the most direct way is jj new --before k, but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top:.

If you enjoy using TUIs, jj arrange provides a commit graph editor similar to git rebase -i for reordering commits.

If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash:.

jj will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message.

Recent findings suggest that to drop a commit from the graph, we can use jj abandon. Let’s drop the preparation commit:.

To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the jj diffedit TUI (see docs).

In a recent development, the jj split TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with jj split -r k:.

Industry observers note that the jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review.

In a recent development, jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:.

Now jj log reveals our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated:.

Sources indicate that we’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like /.

Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

To upgrade a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create fresh commits and move the bookmark forward.

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

First, create a new commit on top of our branch. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files.

In a recent development, then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

In a recent development, squash them into the bookmark branch. $ jj squash --from @ --into push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature.

We now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. $ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b].

The remote branch now reflects the fresh changes. The above output notes that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

In this flow, we add newly introduced commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Recent findings suggest that let’s first prepare the new commit. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

The bookmark does not automatically move to our newly introduced commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:.

There are several ways to move the bookmark to the fresh commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:.

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:.

And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch:.

Industry observers note that our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git’s “current branch” state.

Recent findings suggest that syncing with the trunk (e.g. main) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to enhancement our main to the upstream main, and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a upcoming main:.

Sources indicate that jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:.

You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

Sources indicate that large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say we’re building a fresh feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:.

Recent findings suggest that jj’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:.

In a recent development, after you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

In a recent development, it’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a newly introduced report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a latest Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which rolled out only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

It has been revealed that apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That noted, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

In a recent development, when it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less crucial in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

  • At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

In a recent development, consumers can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot presently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for customers running the public version without requiring another app enhancement.

To read WABetaInfo‘s full report, follow this link.

The Strongest Sokoban Solver

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healeycodes

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, soksolv solves more levels than any published Sokoban solver on both standard benchmark suites, including 24 world-first automated level solves.
  • As is common for this era, I did not handwrite a single line of code.
  • I ran the 14-day long Claude session from my MacBook and did ~50% of the work on-the-go by dictating to my iPhone via /remote-control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, soksolv solves more levels than any published Sokoban solver on both standard benchmark suites, including 24 world-first automated level solves. It's also faster on the levels that other solvers solve (~3.2x in total time).

As is common for this era, I did not handwrite a single line of code. I used one long Opus 5.5 session in Claude Code, along with ~430 subagents (a mixture of Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.2) for an API-equivalent cost ~$3,500 (I used the $100 initiative, and a reset).

I ran the 14-day long Claude session from my MacBook and did ~50% of the work on-the-go by dictating to my iPhone via /remote-control. On the compute side, I needed 15,000 vCPU-hours (AMD EPYC) to do research and verification runs, as well as the (very) long benchmark runs.

First published in Japan in 1982, Sokoban is a puzzle game where you push boxes onto goals. It was proven PSPACE-complete in 1997, and small boards hide massive search spaces. Human-solvable levels commonly need hundreds to thousands of moves.

Below is the solution for Microban #1.

Sokoban levels can be explored as a cyclic graph of moves. With a branching factor of ~16 (but up to ~176 on huge boards!), any kind of brute forcing becomes unviable after a handful of moves.

Recent findings suggest that as a player, and especially as a solver author, Sokoban levels feel adversarial by design. Any obvious heuristic is immediately punished by the game rules or the level author.

Recent findings suggest that when I wrote my first Sokoban solver (~4 years ago), I tried to encode how I thought I was playing the game. Without thinking too hard, we can describe this as "get the boxes to the goals". Okay, so, how do we calculate that in a program? Maybe the sum of box-to-goal distances?

Using this as a guide, we can explore the graph of possible moves and see what happens.

Ah, by prioritizing boxes on goals we walk right into a trap. The game becomes deadlocked and unsolvable, and our solver with a single rule runs until the end-of-time with no solution.

We'll need to come up with a bag of strategies to perform better than even novice players.

It has been revealed that I've been using frontier agents at work for a while now and I enjoy (and get a lot of profit from) what I call "creative goal setting". Where you define the goal, parts of the path, risks that you consider acceptable, and some preferences on the method.

In a recent development, what I've experienced, is that agents are really great hill-climbers, and a solver program is the purest hill there is. There are two things to measure: the number of levels solved, and some kind of aggregate time of those solutions.

At the beginning of this project, I started a Claude Code session and defined a hill climbing blueprint. One immutable incumbent version of the solver (the first version was just a brute force search), one hypothesis per experiment, a frozen verifier (so agents don't cheat), and separate promotion suites.

Industry observers note that as I continued to make progress, I expanded the pool of levels that I measured my solver against until I was taking on the two common benchmarks used in the Sokoban solver community; the Large Test Suite and the Open Test Suite, which contain increasingly complex Sokoban levels. There are some duplicate levels between the suites with a unique count of 9,756 total levels, with an average of 16 boxes, and ~830 moves (~160 pushes) to solve each.

I knew that I didn't want to build on top of an existing solver for two reasons. The first was that I did this project because I love this kinda stuff, and it's a less interesting journey to make small patches to an existing program. It's much more fun to be part of something from scratch and to live the narrative of it.

The second reason, that I didn't realize until the ending stages of the project, was that if you build on top of existing solution, you become extremely tied to certain design decisions without the knowledge of those decisions, and it becomes impossible to make improvements beyond one order of magnitude.

So I set some initial ground rules for the agents. No machine learning (much harder for me to audit), no reading the code of rival solvers (or we risk copying inefficient designs), and no hardcoding to solve levels (that's cheating).

Industry observers note that at the beginning of the project, I was concerned about agents cheating. I'm sure we all remember early LLM generations that would just comment out tests to achieve their given goals!

Industry observers note that but I found no signs of agents cheating at all. My best guess for this is that I steered agent motivation towards experimentation and learning rather than it being a pure numbers game.

Two more ground rules that I set were: the solver must be written in Go (I find it fun to read), and a 15 GB memory cap so it fits on an 8-core/16 GB machine. I also wanted to use the same cores as Festival (the leading rival solver) for matters of fairness.

During the iteration cycle, each solution was replayed move by move on the original level using the frozen verifier.

Recent findings suggest that the verifier lives in its own package and agents weren't allowed to edit it. I also had a similar check when promoting fresh pruning rules. I had 2,632 known solutions that were replayed through it and if the prune cut a single known solution then it was failed (this ended up catching two unsound pruning rules before they landed).

So earlier I spoke about solving levels as being like exploring a graph, right? And you probably counted each node as being a worker step or a box move. But walking is free! Only pushes change the puzzle. So we search over pushes and treat "where can the worker reach" as a flood fill.

One "position": the box squares and which region the worker is in (not the exact square).

In a recent development, there are many optimizations like this to shrink the search tree of moves. For example, boxes can only be pushed, so when a box is stuck in a tunnel, there are a number of forced pushes that can be collapsed into one macro move, which makes the tree shallower.

My solver had humble beginnings. I started with a best-first search. Expand the most promising positions, and kill positions that create dead squares.

Another obvious optimization is to deduplicate positions. Two positions are the same if the boxes are on the same squares and the worker can walk to the same boxes.

In a recent development, the worker can stand anywhere it can walk to and it's still the same position. So I store the worker as the first square of the area it can reach (top-left wins), and all of those collapse into one entry. The right side of the diagram roughly indicates this can be stored efficiently in memory.

Industry observers note that one lesson that I learned early on is that most of the search area is dead! But outside of the obvious cases, it's either difficult to see at first that it is dead, or it comes with a cost (node searches) to figure out that it is in fact dead.

There are the simple deadlock cases:.

It has been revealed that there are simple deadlock squares. For example, here on Holland #68, 19 of the 69 floor squares can never hold a box:.

A more advanced technique that relates to deadlocks is called PI-corral pruning (Push-In corral) where a corral is a region the worker cannot reach because there are boxes in the way.

The insight here is that these corrals must eventually be dealt with and so the solver can prioritize pushes into them which may prune other moves that postpone this work.

In other words, there's no point spending time solving one half of the level if there's a small number of forced moves that may make the original position dead!

The three boxes on the right fence off an area the worker can't reach. Every push of those boxes goes into that area, so nothing else on the board can help until one of them moves, which leaves 3 pushes worth trying instead of 7.

Sources indicate that many levels have a concept of "goal rooms" where every box ends up clustered in the same area. Solvers need to carefully consider the packing order of goals in order to reduce the search area. The number of fill orders is roughly n! for n goals (10 goals ≈ 3.6 million orders), and for some levels, most of those will lead to deadlocks.

If the first box stops on the nearest goal then it parks right in the doorway, blocking the other two from getting past it.

A really cool insight into Sokoban solvers is that you can search backwards from the solved position by pulling boxes. Just to be ultra clear here, as you may be skim reading, in the game Sokoban, you cannot ever pull a box. However, by simulating pulls, you are effectively rewinding time of a potential solution. A forward and backward search that meet in the middle need significantly less positions than either alone.

Industry observers note that going forwards, a box pushed into a corner is stuck there for good so many squares are dead ends. Going backwards you pull boxes and you can always pull a box back out of a corner. So on this board, the backwards search has no dead squares at all.

Consider again the branching factor of ~16 that I mentioned. Each additional deepening increases the search area. So if you can start at both ends at once, then each search tree is cut to half of the depth (b^d nodes become about 2*b^(d/2)). As we can see here on Microban #5.

Feature Space Search (FESS) was used by the first solver to solve the 90 XSokoban levels (a benchmark once out of reach for computers). The paper is incredibly interesting and clear and approachable (it's also not math-heavy!). I really recommend reading it directly but I will also summarize the key concepts here.

I should also note that the primary author of the FESS paper, Yaron Shoham, is also the author of the very-strong Sokoban solver Festival, of which my solver is greatly indebted to the methods of.

I think the best way to explain FESS is to compare it against best-first search. So, instead of prioritizing a single node-score (calculated from some useful metrics) and using that to guide the search, FESS instead:.

To better explain these "features", let's take a look at Holland #68 after 38 of 261 pushes.

And then, a concrete example to show the efficiency gains is to look at how the search area is expanded on Microban #35 with best-first compared against FESS.

Here's the same level searched two different ways. Each cell in the grid is one combination of features: boxes on goals across, and worker areas up. The number in the cell is how many positions the search has expanded there so far. Best-first always picks the position with the lowest estimate (on this level that means it camps in one cell and spends 405 of its 1259 expansions there). FESS takes turns instead and alternates with the best cell so far and it's done in 823 expansions instead.

Although, to be fair, on most of the small Microban levels like this one, best-first is usually quicker. FESS does best when the estimate is wrong for thousands of positions in a row.

I steered my planning agent to implement directly from the FESS paper on day one as it remains the cutting edge classical search strategy for Sokoban.

On day two of the project, I kicked off a research agent to explore ideas from other domains and to pitch me on some experiment ideas.

This idea of novelty came out of that exploration, which was applied to different areas of my solver to help widen the search area, to hopefully steer different kinds of search into fruitful areas. Novelty comes from classical planning: width-based search / "novelty" by Nir Lipovetzky and Hector Geffner (IW, 2012; best-first width search, 2017).

So to avoid getting stuck in low-value areas of the search tree, novelty can be used to reward positions (or, more abstract states) that have not been seen before.

For example, when choosing between similarly ranked moves, placing a box onto a square that no box has been on so far can aid when trying to make a forward search meet a backward search, because we are widening the so-called "middle".

A position counts as novel if a box lands on a square that no box has touched so far in this search. Novel positions can jump the queue. In this example, it takes 33 expansions with the rule and 73 without.

A heavy steer that I gave my planning agent throughout this project was to make good use of concurrency and I really pushed for communicating, organizing, and re-using work. One of the reasons I pushed in this direction, is that concurrent programming is inherently difficult for humans (but less-so for frontier models) and all the other leading solvers are human written.

Sources indicate that additionally, all serious rival solvers are written in languages where it is hard to write fast and correct concurrent programs like C and C++. So I believed that my steering here would give me an uneven edge over the rivals.

Thus, my solver makes great use of a lane architecture. Many different searches run in parallel on all 8 cores and help each other. Festival also uses this concept.

Sources indicate that A lane is one search configuration on its own core with its own memory share. They publish positions into shared tables (to meet each other), share deadlocks, and depending on their progress, they lend each other memory.

For example, on Holland #68, no single lane is able to solve it within 10 sec but together the lanes finish it in 3.8 sec!

This lane architecture is a key strategy to fight against the difficulty of the adversial-seeming levels of Sokoban.

Very often, no single lane is able to make progress but as lanes prioritize different areas of the search tree, with each making unique decisions, they end up collaborating over and over again.

Through testing, I found that it's important to keep a balance of forward lanes and backwards lanes. A concept that frequently occurred in my research was to make connections between different kinds of work.

In a recent development, A positions hash decides where it goes in the table. The tables are a fixed size so a fresh entry can land of top of an old one, which is fine in practice. The worst that happens is we miss a meeting that we could have had (but the new meeting is fine too!). For example, on Grigr2002 #17, the lanes posted 8 possible meets, 1 checked out, and the level was solved in 0.65 seconds.

As I mentioned before, one kind of "speed limit" on travelling through the search space is having to do work in order to discover deadlocks.

Along with valid positions, that are aiming to meet in the middle and connect a solution together, deadlock positions are also shared in order skip duplicated work.

Later, when another lane runs into the same three boxes configuration, with the worker on the same normalized square, it can look up the pattern (without searching further ahead!) and skip it because it now knows it's dead.

During the beginning stages of this project, I wanted to see how my planner agent and its research subagents would make progress without copying ideas directly from existing solvers. This got us pretty far, and we were able to solve ~93% of the benchmark levels at that point.

But eventually we hit diminishing returns and it was time to draw on every possible signal; reading through existing codebases, and altering them to leave behind "search traces" for analysis by frontier models. Tearing down my initial ground rules that banned such actions.

According to recent reports, one research agent spent some time analyzing which levels that Sokolution was able to solve (levels that no other solver was able to solve). The odd thing was that it solved these seemingly complex-for-other-solver levels very rapidly, in a handful of seconds. The theory the research agent came up with was that (due to the level layout) Sokolution was factoring the levels, by which we mean that it is splitting the levels into different parts that can effectively be solved independently.

Industry observers note that by separating the task into multiple search trees, it reduces the depth of each tree and helps avoid the deadly branching factor. Now, this strategy is less strong (or doesn't apply) to many other levels (mostly Life, Premysl Zika, and Secundus gradus ad Olympo groups). But on the levels that it can solve, it performs well as part of a portfolio of other strategies that the solver employs.

There are different ways that levels can be separated like this. One common method is that you can count dead box areas as walls (since boxes may never cross such a boundary) and slice up it into multiple search trees.

As you may be picking up by now, most strategies are interested in shrinking the search area, smaller and smaller, until we're able to walk right up to the solution.

Recent findings suggest that which brings us to relays. This strategy comes into play when a lane gets stuck close to the goal. For example, if a good number of boxes have been placed on goals already, the whole portfolio of strategies can be restarted on the best board state that has been seen. With the finished boxes becoming walls!

This was one of the later experiments, when we were really grinding to break through some of the "gap" levels (levels that other solvers solved but at that point we did not). Its discovery was rewarded by 7 level solves.

In a recent development, the software factory (if you will) ran like this. There was one planning agent (Opus 5.5) that ran on a heartbeat check of 15min which checked on in-flight experiments and the health/connectivity of VMs. This planning agent was tasked with driving us forward. It listened to my setup instructions (a rough design of how I wanted to hillclimb, ground rules, general direction) and then picked experiments, analyzed results, and promoted winners.

There were then two types of subagents:.

Recent findings suggest that another design I asked to be implemented was a level ledger as the single-source of truth when it came to our capabilities per level. For example, we needed to track which levels had been solved, which levels regressed, which were fast and slow. Certain families of levels received tags and helped inform the research direction based on the potential impact of wins.

When I was able to be more active, I would ask the planning agent to pitch me on ideas so I could inspect and steer the direction we were building towards but overnight I would give it permission to drive and make larger decisions.

Industry observers note that one of the areas that I added a lot of value was when it came to risk. All the agents seemed extremely uncomfortable with taking on any amount of risk (even when I specifically asked them to take it on). The agents were petrified about regressions or their analysis being incorrect. I suppose they felt like this because they had all the tools they needed to be 100% correct. The only problem was that this would have cost an immense amount of wallclock time.

Planner: You're right about my tendency to over-verify.

Sources indicate that A full 600 sec run of the two level suites takes ~85 hours per 8-core/16 GB slice of a VM! I had to set in place many mechanisms to restrict the agents wallclock spend like forcing all commands to have certain timeouts, spawning many research agents to search for ways to get signals from testing runs without spending the entire time (e.g. scoring progress before actually hitting the goal, and measuring how closely we followed known solution paths).

Without heavy steering when it came to wallclock time, my gut-feel is that this project could have lasted 10x as long as it did (which would have extended it to just under half a year).

According to recent reports, another problem was that agents are all too happy to seek 1% improvements over and over. They crave anything to make progress towards overall goals. The problem is that this domain demanded far more aggressive thinking and experimentation (again, something agents can be weaker at).

Many of my steers were to kill off different kinds of research that were thinking too small, that were just iterating on ideas that didn't feel strong enough to take us the whole way.

It has been revealed that early on in the project, I set strict gates on what an experimented needed to prove in order to earn a promotion. They needed to result in "10% gains" meaning level performance, or progress towards solving trimmed level suites. With a minimum of +3 newly introduced levels solved for each and almost no regressions.

According to recent reports, towards the middle of the project, with much of the low hanging fruit gone, I steered the planning agent to spend time thinking about cheap gates that could be ran before a full implementation and a partial benchmarking run. This was extremely profitable and helped increase progress-per-wallclock during the middle section of the project.

Another thing that I heavily steered was asking for more experiments to be put in flight even if they had slightly overlapping areas of interest. The planner preferred to wait for results but, again, this cost too much wallclock time. The tokens were far cheaper than the compute, so better to spend and waste tokens, than spend and waste wallclock time and compute.

You can see the cheap gates arrive on Nov 5 and then from then onwards, most failed ideas died at the gate (orange) before they ever made it to a fuller test phase (red).

In the final quarter of the project, a lot of this had to be teared down. The mid-hanging fruit was gone, regressions were common, and the bets were far more difficult to find. Also, the gains that we were looking for were far smaller too. I'd guess that the time-per-experiment increased by a factor of ~5, due to the additional testing and verification that was required.

Industry observers note that to go back to heuristics for a sec, there was one day during the project where we got stuck on a large group of levels that started with boxes already on goals. You'd think that "boxes on goals" would be the gold standard of Sokoban heuristics to follow but it turns out to be a lot more complicated than that.

11% of the benchmark levels start with 75% or more of their boxes already on goals! And boy did this mess with our heuristics. Every progress signal (boxes on goals, goal distance, packing order) all noted that we were very near the finish, except a "jumbling" of the level was required.

Some naive experiments swiftly failed like "unpack first" or lowering the rewards for boxes on goals.

Finally, a Fable 5.2 analyst was able to break through and pitch a "dive" lane, a greedy search backwards from the solved position that maximized distance from goals with a return phase at the end. The result was that 12 of a cluster of 16 stuck levels became solved.

Recent findings suggest that so, we were never able to make "boxes on goals" stop being a strong signal. Instead, a lane was added that deliberately ignored that advice.

Three of the four boxes here start on goals and it looks nearly done, right? But two of them have to come off before anything else can actually go in. So the count drops 3 → 1 before climbing back to 4.

While the experiments did run their own multi-hour benchmark runs on subsets of level suites, it wasn't until the very end of the project that I asked the planner to take on a full 600 sec benchmark run, which as I noted earlier, takes ~85 hours per VM-slice!

It has been revealed that all this work to just sit and wait and watch the progress and the planner agents projections. My solver ended up losing the first full benchmark by a few levels.

In order to save hundreds of $, I decided to only benchmark against the strongest rival, Festival, and for the others, I trusted their public benchmark numbers. But I knew that I wanted to verify my solver against Festival on like-for-like hardware and configuration.

Being a few levels short, or even a few levels over, was clearly not good enough. It was within the noise threshold, so back to the design board we went.

After further experiments and promotions, it was time to run the final benchmark. 8 dedicated cores and a 15 GB cgroup each, along with each solution being verified. My solver pulled ahead, beyond the noise threshold, to just enough to be able to claim victory: +10 on LTS and +18 on OTS (full results).

I've gone with a somewhat spiky claim in this article, stating that my solver is the strongest in the world, and I believe I have a pretty good claim to it.

According to recent reports, note: charts and numbers in this post use Festival measured on our hardware at every limit (+10 LTS / +18 OTS at 10 min). Where charts reference rivals, they use their published numbers (from other benchmarks) because I could not afford the compute to be thorough. Full benchmark results, with per-level times, are in the repo.

According to recent reports, median time per solved board is 0.05 sec (ours) vs. 1.00 sec (Festival). On the 9,223 levels that both solver solve, there's a 4.40 sec vs 14.16 sec mean, and ours is faster on 8,809 (96%).

Additionally, my solver achieves 24 world-first automated solves (especially in the Premysl Zika and Sven Egevad family).

Against the community (unverified numbers aside from Festival), we also rank very well (see diagram at top of post).

I would be interested to know if you could one-shot this project with a prompt. I suspect so. Something like "Fable, here's unlimited compute, build the best Sokoban solver".

In a recent development, however, I think it comes down to efficiency. Without a human driver, I strongly believe the wallclock time (and therefore the compute costs) would be in the 100x range. Validating each of the 792 experiments the proper way would take ~67,000 VM-slice hours, or ~$20,000 at market prices. Or, ~230 days of wall-clock in the VM configuration that I ran.

During this project, I felt a little closer to a technical manager than an IC; following, steering, and guiding. It's kinda like managing a team of strong engineers. Sure, they can go off path and waste some time, but a light steer will fix it.

Recent findings suggest that writing a solver is extremely agent-friendly. The results are easily verified and there's no human experience to tune for.

This project ultimately felt like a strategy game, something from the Tycoon family. I'm a big computer gamer, and I think this is where I drew some of the motivation from. The methods, the experiments, the results, it all had a physical feeling to me. It felt like a fight.

I think in this agentic age of software, you have to want the goal as much as the agent. Yes, anyone can build software. But you need to care about it, you need to love it. The human focus and effort remains.

In the end it took 388 messages to the planner over 14 days.

This project would not have been possible if Yaron Shoham (Festival, FESS) had not published incredible work, as well as open sourcing a strong solver with multiple releases.

I took deep inspiration from any open source solver that I could find, as well as watching closed-source solver behavior as much as possible. I initially thought I would need to reverse engineer the closed-source ones to cross the finish line but it did not come to pass.

The animations in this article were generated using Fable 5.2 and use the Lager skin by Borgar Þorsteinsson (CC BY 3.0).

While I'm interested in reaching a 100% completion of the benchmark, I will need more compute-efficient strategies to do so.

Sources indicate that as I mentioned, I steered away from some of the known machine learning research that has been applied to Sokoban boards because I wanted a classic solver that was easy to audit. But perhaps there's some interesting strategies and combinations of classic+learning solvers that can be written.

I'm looking for more projects that are shaped like this one, where I can learn more about puzzle solving, and compete with the work of others.

Get the source code for my solver here: https://github.com/healeycodes/soksolv.

  • Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.
  • Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iFixit’s teardown of the latest Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

In a recent development, iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Sources indicate that percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%.

It has been revealed that percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#4589. Why the Airbus A321XLR often gets stuck climbing for first few hours of flight

Why the Airbus A321XLR often gets stuck climbing for first few hours of flight

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Airbus A321XLR is revolutionizing transatlantic travel, but there is a painful catch to its revolutionary range.
  • In a recent development, an airplane cannot just take off and soar to its final cruising altitude on a long-range flight.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the flight progresses, the engines consume fuel at a rate of several tons per hour, causing the aircraft's overall mass to drop steadily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Airbus A321XLR is revolutionizing transatlantic travel, but there is a painful catch to its revolutionary range. It must be trapped at low altitudes for the first few hours of a trip. Since an aircraft's most fuel-efficient altitude varies dynamically as it burns off fuel weight, the long-range narrowbody and many other long-haul aircraft spend a large percentage of their flight time actively rising.

In a recent development, an airplane cannot just take off and soar to its final cruising altitude on a long-range flight. When an airliner first takes off, its fuselage is heavily laden with thousands of gallons of jet fuel required to cross an ocean or reach a distant continent. Step climbing is a dynamic operational technique designed to maximize fuel efficiency by matching an aircraft’s altitude to its changing weight over the course of a long-haul journey.

Recent findings suggest that as the flight progresses, the engines consume fuel at a rate of several tons per hour, causing the aircraft's overall mass to drop steadily. Once the onboard flight computers calculate that the aircraft has shed enough weight to make a higher altitude aerodynamically advantageous, the crew requests permission from air controllers to climb. The flight crew will repeat this entire sequence multiple times during an eight-to-eleven-hour trip, burning off fuel, and stepping up to the next flight level.

It has been revealed that the A321XLR pushes the physical limits of a narrowbody platform, necessitating a performance trade-off between total range and early-flight efficiency and speed. Airbus had to design a jet that could carry payloads in order to convert a domestic workhorse into a single-aisle transatlantic endurance aircraft. The end product is a narrowbody with a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 223,000 lb (101,000 kg), far more than any A321 variant before it.

According to recent reports, the A321XLR cannot effectively climb to higher altitudes at maximum MTOW because it needs a lot of lift to stay airborne until it sheds weight. In the thin, less dense air at cruising flight levels around 37,000 feet (11,200 m), the A321XLR’s wing simply cannot generate enough lift. If the aircraft tries to force its way to these higher altitudes too early, it would have to fly at a high angle of attack. Not only would it result in significant drag and fuel waste, but it would also increase the risk of a stall.

In a recent development, pilots of the A321XLR are specifically warned in official training that early cruising levels will be severely restricted when the aircraft lifts off beyond 85% MTOW, frequently topping out at just 32,000 feet (9,700 meters). Unlike the rocket-like ascent typical of an empty or smaller single-aisle jet, the last stages of reaching those early altitudes are infamously slow, with the climb rate dropping to a taxing 500 feet per minute.

Recent findings suggest that the huge fuel tank built right into the cargo bay of the A321XLR is responsible for its enormous range. Depending on the mission, airlines could install or delete optional auxiliary center tanks in the belly hold of earlier long-range models, such as the A321LR. Airbus abandoned this modular strategy for the XLR and completely reworked the bottom fuselage. The airplane has an enormous overall capacity of almost 10,500 gallons (39,747 liters) when the conventional wing and center tanks are added.

Recent findings suggest that behind the main landing gear compartment is the jet's conformal Rear Center Tank. By making the tank walls an integral part of the airplane's structural shell, Airbus maximized fuel volume without eating up all the underfloor baggage space. This specialized tank design allows the narrowbody to carry an extra 3,408 gallons (12,900 liters) of fuel.

While this engineering feat unlocks an 11-hour, 4,700-nautical-mile range, it creates a severe weight-and-balance headache the moment those tanks are topped off. Because the RCT is physically welded into the aft fuselage, the aircraft carries a permanent structural weight penalty even when flying empty. If an airline flies the XLR on a short 2-hour domestic hop with the rear tank empty, it must burn extra fuel just to carry the dead weight.

According to recent reports, to overcome the weight of its massive fuel load, the A321XLR must perform a calculated, multi-hour sequence with air traffic control known as step climbing. The flight crew must climb to a lower, temporary altitude, level off, and wait. Airbus flight manuals explicitly dictate this step-climbing technique for the XLR to keep the aircraft flying as close to its dynamically shifting optimum altitude as possible throughout a long-range mission.

This process is a slow-motion game dictated by the jet's fuel burn rate. The A321XLR consumes fuel rapidly early in the flight, about 5,000 lb (2,250 kg) of fuel every hour. As this weight burns off, the aircraft's total mass drops, the wings require less lift to maintain level flight, and the optimum cruising altitude rises. For every few tons of fuel burned, the pilots request a step-up in increments of 2,000 feet (600 m) on average.

On a typical ten-hour transatlantic crossing, an A321XLR crew will execute one or two of these step climbs before reaching their final, most efficient cruising altitude. Managing these steps requires constant coordination with air traffic controllers, who must find an open slot in the North Atlantic tracks.

Sources indicate that forcing a heavy A321XLR to its optimum altitude too early can trap pilots in a high-altitude aerodynamic bottleneck known as the 'coffin corner,' where the margin between flying and stalling virtually disappears. Officially called the 'q-corner,' this phenomenon occurs when an aircraft is flying at high altitudes where the air is thin.

In a recent development, there, the wings require a higher speed to produce enough lift, and the aircraft's minimum safe speed, or stall speed, rises. At the same time, the speed of sound decreases in the cold, high-altitude air, lowering the aircraft's maximum safe speed. That is the critical Mach number, where air flowing over the wing goes supersonic and causes violent structural buffeting.

In a recent development, for a heavily loaded narrowbody like the A321XLR climbing up in altitude, these two speeds begin to draw together, creating a dangerously narrow operational envelope. If a pilot flies too slowly, the heavy jet will experience a low-speed stall and fall out of the sky. If they fly too fast, shockwaves forming on the wings will cause high-speed buffeting and a loss of control. When the XLR takes off near its MTOW limit, trying to push past 32,000 feet (9,750 m) early in the flight shrinks this buffer down to a razor-thin margin of just a few knots. To avoid risk, training notes and standard operating procedures heavily caution crews against chasing the theoretical optimum altitude too aggressively.

This aerodynamic trap becomes much more acute when the aircraft encounters high-altitude turbulence or mountain waves. A sudden updraft or downdraft can instantaneously shift the angle of airflow over the wings, instantly pushing the aircraft outside its narrow safe-speed envelope. Thus, pilots will deliberately choose to fly 2,000 feet below the aircraft's technical capability, trading fuel efficiency for a safety buffer.

Operating thousands of feet below optimal cruise levels forces the A321XLR to plow through significantly denser air, increasing aerodynamic drag and hiking fuel consumption by an estimated 2.5% per hour. For airline accountants managing razor-thin margins on a 4,700-nautical-mile route, these initial hours of flight represent a concentrated period of fuel inefficiency. However, it is an unavoidable 'cost of doing business.'.

Industry observers note that while lingering in the thicker air of the lower flight levels levies a performance penalty on the plane, it inadvertently creates a widebody-style comfort upgrade that complements the A321XLR passenger experience. When an aircraft cannot climb to its optimal altitude, it pays for that safety buffer in fuel. However, this inefficiency unlocks a human benefit inside the cabin.

In a recent development, typical narrowbody aircraft cruising at high altitudes maintain an internal cabin pressure equivalent to being on top of an 8,000-foot (2,400 m) mountain. This thin cabin air is the primary culprit behind the deep physical exhaustion, pounding headaches, and severe dehydration associated with jet lag. As the A321XLR spends its heaviest initial cruise hours lower down, the equivalent altitude inside the fuselage is much lower, closer to 6,000 feet (1,800 m).

Airbus capitalized on this inevitable flight profile by integrating a upcoming cabin pressure control standard in the Airspace Cabin. As the structural pressure differential between the inside and outside the plane doesn't have to be stretched to its absolute breaking point, the system can safely schedule a lower cabin altitude.

Industry observers note that this dense, humid air matches the comfortable profile of an advanced widebody like Airbus' own A350 series. Passengers stepping off a transoceanic or intercontinental flight arrive feeling more refreshed than they would on an older Boeing 757, turning a performance compromise into a major traveler advantage that has helped shape how airlines market and deploy the jet worldwide.

Goodbye to Kyle Richards' life before grandchildren.

The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star and husband Mauricio Umansky became grandparents after her daughter Farrah Aldjufrie gave birth to her and boyfriend Zach Goldsmith's baby boy Brooks Steele Goldsmith.

In a recent development, "The birth was extremely easy, peaceful, seamless and happy," Farrah told People in an article published Nov. 20. "We had a party at the hospital and watched the sun come up after he was born. The transition has felt very natural. The house has been crowded with family giving so much love and support. We feel beyond lucky.”.

Days before the reality TV family—also including Kyle's younger daughters Alexia, 30, Sophia, 26 and Portia, 18, with Mauricio—shared the news, the Bravo personality shared her excitement about the new addition.

According to recent reports, apple today confirmed that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a upcoming post published on its developer portal, Apple today declared a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the tech giant, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple stated that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

It has been revealed that apple added that a upcoming “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and upgrade their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB initiative to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the manufacturer’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances ….

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud looks.

It has been revealed that however, tucked away in the small print in the tech giant’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

According to recent reports, siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust concerns. Essentially, Apple believes that if it debuts Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:.

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:.

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of problems.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The tech giant may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

According to recent reports, A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest ….

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated problems coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication problem affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio mentioned […].

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”.

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Industry observers note that democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (481 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • Industry observers note that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's key to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

Industry observers note that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that organization or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Industry observers note that next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams
